title: Ocean Acidification: Foundations
welcome_lead: Plunge into how CO2 lowers ocean pH and threatens coral reefs.
meta_desc: GCSE Environmental Science adventure on ocean acidification foundations: pH change and CO2 dissolution.
final_note: You can now explain why fizzy oceans spell trouble for corals.

walkthroughs.body_html: Oceans absorb roughly a quarter of human CO2 emissions. Dissolved CO2 reacts with water: CO2 + H2O gives H2CO3 (carbonic acid), which dissociates into H+ and HCO3- (bicarbonate). More H+ ions mean lower pH. Pre-industrial surface pH was around 8.2; today it is about 8.1, a 30 percent rise in acidity.

Corals and shellfish build skeletons and shells from calcium carbonate. Acidification reduces carbonate ion availability, making it harder and more energy-costly to build CaCO3. Bleaching occurs when corals expel their symbiotic algae under heat or chemical stress, losing their colour and food source. Repeated bleaching kills reefs.

pH is logarithmic, so a drop of 0.1 means about 26 percent more H+ ions. Oceans naturally buffer through carbonate chemistry, but the rate of CO2 emissions exceeds buffering capacity, allowing acidification to occur. The 0.1 unit fall from pH 8.2 to 8.1 since 1750 represents a roughly 30 percent increase in acidity.
